title: Is Forgotten Island Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Joyful Film
text:
Is Forgotten Island Worth Watching? Our Honest Review Of The Joyful Film

Forgotten Island feels like a return to when animated films were truly special, with something extra layered on top. While Pixar has been slowly going downhill a bit (remember when every single Pixar film hit?), this family movie is joyful, hilarious and will bring many people to tears. It follows best friends Jo (H.E.R) and Raissa (Liza Soberano) as they find themselves stuck in the mysterious world of Nakali. Based on Filipino folklore, the pair encounter different monsters, creatures and animals along the way.

In a sort of mashup of The Hangover and Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, Jo and Raissa can’t remember what happened the night before. Soon, they face a harsh truth: if they don’t return home, they may forget the most important memory of all… their friendship.

Entertainment writers Bernice Corral and Rachel Choy sat down to discuss Forgotten Island, including what made it so memorable (we won’t be forgetting Forgotten Island!), how meaningful it was to see the Philippines portrayed in a positive light, and whether it’s going to be the next big hit.

Rachel Choy: Did you know much about Forgotten Island before going to watch it?

Bernice Corral: When the announcement that Liza Soberano was going to be part of it, I was very excited for that. I’ve been following her for so long, and I knew she had been trying to make it in Hollywood from the Philippines. And then, obviously, seeing so many Filipinos involved like H.E.R, Lea Salonga, Dolly de Leon, and Manny Jacinto, I was very excited.

RC: What were your initial thoughts when watching?

BC: I love the animation style! I’m such an animation lover, and it reminded me a lot of SpiderVerse. Also, side note: whenever Southeast Asia is portrayed in any Hollywood film, they put this yellow filter over it to show that it’s a poor country. So to see the Philippines in such a vibrant way, was amazing.

RC: There’s racism to that, with the yellow filter and how SE Asia is portrayed, for sure.

BC: To see a powerful and actual reflection of the Philippines was very heartwarming.

RC: The animation was so cool, and the color scheme as well; the neon and bright colors! It was so saturated. I also loved the mix of 3D animation and back to 2D. And the flashback to cartoons we watched growing up like Dragon Ball Z and Sailor Moon.

BC: It was so nostalgic.

RC: It honestly was. I was sitting there thinking, am I watching him transform into a Super Saiyan right now? What’s going on! There are also so many Filipino references and the odd Tagalog words or phrases, but there aren’t English subtitles. It’s not dumbed down for the audience. I thought it was really awesome. I can’t speak the language, but I got the gist of those parts. I may have missed out on little things that are Easter eggs just for Filipino people, but I still loved it.

BC: There were still the context clues and the inflections of how lines were delivered. I could understand it, but I agree. I think the voice acting as well was so good and helped to keep those moments universal.

RC: There’s also the little things that are universal across different cultures. Like when Lola throws her sandal at the neighbor.

BC: It’s called the tsinelas. They released a clip of the party scene, and I’m seeing a lot of the Latin communities being like, oh my God, like we’re cousins with the Philippines. It’s obviously transcending Filipino culture. It’s resonating with the Asian community, but also with every other country that Spain colonized.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

RC: I was gonna say, I think we know why. Can we talk about the Jesus picture?

BC: That was one of my favorite parts. As someone who has a painting of the Last Supper hanging in their dining room right now, the use of the Jesus picture itself was so Filipino, but also Jo’s character, where she looks at it and goes, “Sup Jesus”. I feel like it’s such a funny way to portray some Filipinos’ relationships with religion. In the Philippines, Catholicism is so intertwined with our culture, and it’s more part of the culture than actually spiritual. Also loved how the Jesus was in front of the lechon (suckling pig).

RC: I guess because religion came with the colonizers, so it’s a very complicated history. Maybe that’s why it was so cool that the film went into Filipino folklore, which would have been more of the stories that were told before the colonizers came.

BC: I loved it because I don’t actually know much about Filipino folklore aside from specific monsters. They used folklore from different regions. So it’s not just one animal that represents the entire country. I read that Batiba’s folklore is from the Ilocos region, which is where my mum is from. I think it’s also that there are so many subcultures in the Philippines. We’re a whole archipelago, so it’s not just one Filipino story, and they were very self-aware about that. Seeing them do that, along with the other little traits and quirks, was a good way to address that. The Philippines isn’t just one culture.

RC: But aside from the celebration of Filipino culture, it’s also just a really good movie.

BC: Exactly! The themes of friendship and moving abroad can also resonate with a lot of people. And for a lot of people, especially immigrants, it’s about not wanting to forget where you came from. But as time passes by, you can’t remember everything.

RC: Also! It’s a kids’ movie which puts friendship at the centre, and they’re not chasing a man.

BC: They’re chasing each other.

RC: So many movies are always about finding validation from a man.

BC: Not only was it like an exploration of love through friendship, but the flashbacks to Jo and her Lola were so special. I feel like those familial bonds are so important in Filipino culture as well. So it was an exploration of familial love.

RC: I feel like in Asian culture, you have stronger bonds with your grandparents. You’re more likely to have them living with you when you’re growing up, compared to white people.

BC: Yeah, my grandparents took care of me when my parents were at work.

RC: And then on a deeper level, you didn’t have anything like this growing up as a Filipino kid. I had Mulan, which also came with some problematic things, but I still had something.

BC: I would look to Mulan; I would look to Pocahontas and Jasmine because of the brown skin. Even Snow White, because she had black hair. That’s how desperate I was for any representation as a child.

RC: Do you think this film will become important for young Filipino kids?

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

BC: I hope my goddaughter likes this, because her favorite movie is Frozen and I’m like, girl, no, you gotta get around Forgotten Island. I hope she enjoys it and sees herself in it as well.

RC: The other thing is that the creative team are mostly Filipino.

BC: What I loved about it is they employed a Manila-based animation studio, which I think is so cool, because I feel like the arts aren’t taken seriously in the Philippines in the same way, with like a lot of Asian culture. They’d rather you be a doctor or a lawyer or a dentist. So the fact that they’re supporting the arts in the Philippines makes me really happy. And then the score, the composer is Filipino, and he used all Filipino musicians for the score as well. So BINI and SB19 are P-pop groups in the Philippines, and then Sophia from KATSEYE is Filipino, and H.E.R and Liza did the theme song for the movie as well. It’s Filipino in all aspects, and throughout the project, which I love. It translates so well with the movie because you can tell how much love was put into it, and it also speaks to what happens when you actually tap into the people behind the culture when you’re telling a cultural story.

RC: Yeah, because if you have white people telling a cultural story, they’re basically colonising it, and it happens all the time. That can be, like, in a publication, a book, or in movies or whatever. It’s their version of it, which is not real.

BC: I read the production notes, and Januel and Joel said they wrote the characters based on people in their lives.

RC: The only thing is, I don’t think the trailer does it justice. I hope people get past that and go and watch it. It’s such a good movie. I think it could stand the test of time.

BC: I’m hoping it becomes kind of (not to compare Asian movies, but…) K-Pop Demon Hunters, where the popularity grows through word of mouth.

RC: Yes, and it blows up! This is refreshing. Pixar has had a few flops, so it’s time for DreamWorks to come in. I’m a How To Train Your Dragon truther.

BC: Yes, it’s Forgotten Island and then Shrek 5! Please, everyone, support this film if you want to support Asian culture. If you found yourself at a very Asian time in your life this year, and you actually want to support Asian culture, you’ll watch it, and not just use us for clout.

RC: If you don’t watch Forgotten Island, it means you hate Filipinos. So go watch it. Cameron Diaz wants you to watch it.

BC: She grew up with a lot of Filipinos. Lumpia. Adobo.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Forgotten Island is in theaters now.

title: Lili Reinhart On What The Love Hypothesis Movie Changed From The Book: “You Can’t Put Every Single Thing In”
text:
Lili Reinhart On What The Love Hypothesis Movie Changed From The Book: “You Can’t Put Every Single Thing In”

BookTokers have a lot of opinions. Especially when it comes to their beloved books, such as The Love Hypothesis by Ali Hazelwood. The IP is rooted in fandom and began as a Reylo (Rey and Kylo Ren from Star Wars) fanfic before turning into the fake-dating story that spent weeks on the New York Times Best Sellers list. Now it’s had the movie treatment, with Lili Reinhart playing Olive Smith and Tom Bateman playing Dr Adam Carlsen. However, fitting a 300-400 page book into a film comes with sacrifices, and the cast knows how particular the audience is.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Refinery29 Australia (@refinery29au)

“I don’t really know why they chose which scenes [would make it in], but I think it’s just the ones that kind of jump off the page that feel the most cinematic as well,” Reinhart tells Refinery29. “You can’t put every single thing in there because sometimes it just wouldn’t work in a movie; it just wouldn’t make sense or flow in the right way that it does when you’re reading something.”

Bateman admits he hadn’t read the book before he read the script, but believes viewers will appreciate how it stands on its own. “I remember thinking I didn’t feel like there were any holes in the script. The script was such a wonderful page turner. I thought there was everything there that you’d want from a romantic comedy film,” he says. “When I then went and read the book, I thought, yeah, you could have put those moments in, but to be honest, I can see why they didn’t.”

Book purists shouldn’t panic, though, as Reinhart is chronically online and pushed for certain book moments to be added to the script after she joined the project. “I was [for] research purposes seeing sort of the scenes and the lines that people really wanted, and I would push for those. They were mostly already actually in there, but maybe a few lines here and there I pushed for,” she adds. “I was able to give my input and notes on Olive and certain things that maybe I felt lines-wise from the book that people would really want.”

The pair know immense criticism will come from those who love the book, but there’s no such thing as a 100% faithful adaptation, especially when everyone interprets the source text differently. “You can hate the movie if you want. Totally fine,” Reinhart says. “It’s par for the course when you do an adaptation. You genuinely know that some people are not going to like it, and not approve of you as this character that they have been thinking about in their head.” She notes that fans can still go back and read the book, so they can keep loving whatever version they please. The idea of being crucified online for an adaptation doesn’t bother her, either, because as an actor, nothing will stop her from doing her best to play Olive in the way she believes works.

Bateman agrees, saying: “Ultimately, you can’t please everyone. You never will be able to. There’s never been any piece of thing created that was universally loved… but you[‘ve] just got to keep true to yourself.”

One much-loved moment that did make it into The Love Hypothesis movie was Fluchella, where Olive forces Dr Carlsen to get a flu shot. It helps expose Adam’s vulnerabilities and takes their relationship to the next level. “It does so many things in that one moment. Olive gets to see a side of him that he’s still trying to protect,” Bateman muses. “There’s a playfulness there that comes out, but you’ve still got the rigidity of who these characters are.”

The actor thinks that a good book-to-screen adaptation comes down to “energy”. While not all book scenes work on camera, creative teams and actors can channel the same type of feeling, keeping the adaptation feeling faithful but with the ability to be told in a different medium. “I thought they did a really smart job of blending moments [together],” he says. “It’s all to do with character development and story arc.”

The Love Hypothesis will be released on Prime Video on September 23, 2026.

title: KJ Dillard on Taking Care of Yourself In The Public Eye
text:
KJ Dillard on Taking Care of Yourself In The Public Eye

KJ Dillard is the definition of a multi-hyphenate. Before he became a Summer House fan favorite, KJ was a professional skateboarder, genre-defying musician, and model. How has he managed to achieve all of these dreams so fervently? He won’t allow anyone to put him in a box. Growing up in Kansas and Arizona, KJ learned early on how to adapt to different circumstances. Initially, he was part of a well-to-do community, but his parents’ divorce shifted everything, and he soon found himself in an entirely new world. KJ leaned into his interests and started a band with friends from church, where he rapped and sang as their frontman. He also began to take skateboarding seriously, even though it wasn’t very popular. KJ became engrossed in skate culture, obsessing over its rebellious nature and style. His interest blossomed into a nearly ten-year career as a professional skateboarder, during which he inadvertently invented a never-before-seen trick and attracted the attention of the entire skating community. Like that accidentally career-defining moment, KJ seems destined for greatness, no matter the medium.

As the first Black male Summer House castmate, KJ had to learn to navigate the new world of reality television with millions of eyes watching. Ever graceful, he’s taking the lessons and carrying them into another season. In our conversation, we talk about what it means to give yourself grace when you live and date in the public eye, and how he manages the pressure of being “the first.” KJ models the kind of transparency he hopes inspires other men to open up and share more deeply about what they’re feeling. He opened up about his childhood experiences with living with undiagnosed ADHD and having to live with his grandmother. KJ shares that his love for skateboarding has never left him and now serves as a space for self-care. We also cover his return to music and how excited he is to try a new genre and sound. As is his nature, KJ is turning back to the creative outlets that brought him joy as a kid, except now he’s sharing them with the world.

text:
Sneakerinas Are Trending This Fall—This Is The Pair “It” Girls Love

There’s a trending shoe category competing for space in your fall wardrobes, and it can’t quite decide what it wants to be. Sneakerinas combine the slim, delicate shape of a ballet flat with sportier details traditionally found on sneakers. The result is a shoe that looks slightly strange at first and then suddenly makes perfect sense.

The hybrid is quickly becoming more than a niche runway experiment. Brands across the fashion spectrum, from Nike to Chloé and Louis Vuitton, have released their own interpretations, making a strong case for sneakerinas as one of fall’s biggest footwear trends. But among the growing number of options, VIVAIA’s Carol Sneakerinas are emerging as an early It-girl favorite.

Bella Hadid recently wore the latest black tone pair with knee-high socks, a little black dress, and an oversized tan jacket. It’s exactly the kind of off-duty outfit she does particularly well: seemingly thrown together, slightly unexpected, and somehow cooler because nothing looks overly styled.

According to VIVAIA, the outing marked Hadid’s fourth time stepping out in the brand’s shoes. And she isn’t the only one making a case for the Carol. Lola Tung was photographed wearing VIVAIA’s white Christina Sneakerinas, proving that the brand’s take on the trend works just as well with a lighter, flirtier outfit. Seeing both women reach for VIVAIA’s relatively under-the-radar sneakerinas (in different styles and with their own distinct approaches to getting dressed) makes the trend feel less like a fleeting celebrity moment and more like one worth investing in.

Celebrity sightings alone aren’t enough to make me pull the trigger, but these are the types of shoes that could do double duty in almost any closet. The beauty of the sneakerina trend is that it combines the barely-there silhouette of a ballet flat with the tread and practicality of an actual sneaker. Categorizing it might be confusing, but figuring out what to wear with it isn’t. Try a black pair with jeans and your favorite fall sweater, ortake a cue from Hadid and Tung and style them with a mini dress.

After several seasons dominated by ballet flats, Mary Janes, retro sneakers, and increasingly unconventional shoe hybrids, the line between “pretty” shoes and our practical ones has essentially disappeared. And I’m not mad at it. Sneakerinas land right in the middle, and that’s exactly why they work.

title: NYFW Says Bras Are The New Going-Out Tops
text:
NYFW Says Bras Are The New Going-Out Tops

Over this past summer, bikinis became the new going-out tops. And next, we predict that bras and bralettes will replace traditional tops.

From Off Campus — in which Hannah (played by Ella Bright) regularly wears push-up bras and has thick bra straps peeking out from under her tops — to New York Fashion Week’s Spring/Summer 2027 runways — where many designers notably presented models in statement bralettes — the bra is so back.

Bralettes worn as crop tops, padded balconette bras peeking out of button-downs, and bra straps falling down shoulders: NYFW cemented this fashion trend in one way or another. Brands and designers like Sandy Liang, Khaite, Ella Mae, and 7 For All Mankind particularly opted for flirty lingerie on the runway.

So, whether you’re feeling bold enough to wear a bra as a top for a night out or have just been reminded to refresh your bra drawer with new fashionable styles, read on for outfit inspo, styling suggestions, and our shopping picks.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Bra Straps & Peekaboo Bras

Over 15 NYFW runways showcased bras in one form or another, so here are the highlights and popular styling tips to note. Both Aknvas and 7 For All Mankind presented colorful triangle bralettes under lace dresses or loose layers and skinny scarves. Meanwhile, Altuzarra, Grace Ling, Vettese, and more decided on balconette bras or bandeaus under outerwear. And Ella Mae had a whimsical mix of pink bras with fallen straps worn under and over tops.

Layering is perhaps the safest way to wear an exposed bra out and about. Consider adding a lace bralette under a low-neck blouse or oversized blazer, a bold padded bra beneath sheer mesh or crocheted materials, or colorful bra straps peeking from tank tops. Regardless of the bra silhouette, padding level, fabric, or color you opt for, you can make it as noticeable or obscure as you want with the help of layers.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Bralettes & Bras Worn As Tops

Even bolder, many designers styled bralettes and bras as the focal point of their looks. Kaia Gerber opened the Khaite show with a bang in a white padded bra and high-waisted leather skirt. Sandy Liang, Jane Wade, and Aisling Camps presented several models in torso-baring looks with lightly lined bralettes paired with matching low-rise pants or skirts.

If you too want to follow this simple-yet-bold outfit formula too (especially when the weather gets warmer in the spring), deep V-neck bras and longline bralettes are easy silhouettes to transform into faux crop tops. You can also opt for statement prints or extra-strappy designs for something more dramatic and intentional than a basic, plain push-up or T-shirt bra. Just be sure that, no matter which bra you choose, you wear it with the most important thing: confidence.

title: Libra Season Is Here — & It’s Time For You To Strategize Your Future
text:
Libra Season Is Here — & It’s Time For You To Strategize Your Future

What did the tree say to autumn? Leaf me alone! This joke is going to feel real in the upcoming weeks. Welcome to Libra season — a time of justice and fairness. The sun’s movement on September 22nd kicks off the Fall Equinox, which happens simultaneously, starting a new season. This year, the four-week Libra journey feels like it’s straight out of a melodramatic YA novel with a choose-your-own-adventure finish. 

September 25th is a day to notice and be aware of. The sun in Libra juxtaposes Neptune retrograde in Aries. The unrealistic expectations we may hold apply not only to others but to ourselves. It’s vital to comprehend that while our egos may be inflated or deflated, on September 25th, we embrace love in any form. Being sympathetic to everyone’s causes will be easy because it’ll be hard to resist their charms. We could easily fall head over heels and form enchanting entanglements that lead to whimsical trysts. Although these romantic rendezvous and interludes are met with the best intentions, the upcoming Venus retrograde may bring a fizzle to the sizzle. 

Saturn retrograde in Aries opposes the sun in Libra on October 4th. This transit matters because it can bring workplace issues to the surface. Frustrations with bosses, colleagues, or schedules may set us off, or vice versa. To overcome the obstacles of this astrological aspect, we must focus on the game and not dwell on the minimal consequences that ensue. We might be overly critical and cynical, particularly about how we are progressing compared to others. Instead of being judgmental, we should be understanding and offer kindness — especially to ourselves. The lesson is to embrace our imperfections and the messiness of life. 

Venus’s moonwalk in Scorpio lasts for over 40 days this time around (from October 3rd to November 13th). What makes it particularly pungent is that Venus is the planetary ruler of Libra, so when it’s retrograde during its moment to thrive and shine, it can have immense effects on us earthlings. Venus retrograde in Scorpio is going to make us question who is in our life, especially their value. If they aren’t adding anything positive to our aura or existence, then we might want to put them on ice for a hot minute while we work through our feelings. We may choose to stand back from situations, rather than be 100% in them. 

Mercury dives into Scorpio on September 30th, but the pre-shadow period of its impending retrograde commences on October 4th. Now we will begin to see the story unfold, and it will intensify during Mercury retrograde in Scorpio, which runs from October 24th to November 13th. There will be a lot of confusion and ambiguity about how we want to partner and commit because the Scorpio energy is going to be deep at this moment in Libra season. It’s a warning to slow down and take every moment in stride — even though the cosmos are pressuring us to speed up our decisions — and not push boundaries. Remember, haste makes waste, and stay in your lane. 

As you can see, Libra season isn’t the time to start new projects; it’s a month of reflection and contemplation as we map out our next steps and develop a strategy to move our plans forward. To benefit from the vibe, lean into major self-care, call out personal days that are due, and try to unwind. The energy will bring out the highs and lows of situations, so maintain an equilibrium. IKYK, no matter how the planets are playing and clowning around, Libra season asks us to find balance, and we shall! 

DashDividers_1_500x100

Important Dates for Libra Season:

September 22nd: The sun enters Libra, initiating the Fall Equinox in the Northern Hemisphere.

September 26th: The Harvest Full Moon in Aries is a magical lunation to initiate change. 

September 27th: Mars moves into Leo, making us roar for power.

September 30th: Mercury swims into Scorpio, magnifying our intuition. 

October 3rd: Venus retrograde in Scorpio urges us to re-evaluate our romances and liaisons. 

October 10th: The New Moon in Libra defines who we spend our time with and how.

October 15th: Pluto turns direct, completing the retrograde cycle that began on May 6th. Growth is possible now more than ever.
